The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42)

Pages 31–42 (12 pages)
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 31

The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas In the sensuous sphere there are 12 types of akusala cittas (unwholesome consciousness) that have roots:

a.) cittas rooted in attachment (i.e. with their base or foundation in attachment):

1. citta, unprompted connected with wrong 2. citta, prompted view accompanied by pleasant 3. citta, unprompted feeling. not connected with 4. citta, prompted wrong view 5. citta, unprompted connected with wrong 6. citta, prompted view accompanied by indifferent feeling. 7. citta, unprompted not connected with 8. citta, prompted wrong view

b.) cittas rooted in ill-will or aversion:

9. citta, unprompted accompanied by unpleasant feeling, connected with ill10. citta, prompted will.

c.) cittas rooted in delusion or ignorance:

11. citta, connected with doubt accompanied by indifferent feeling. 12. citta, connected with restlessness

The sensuous sphere: 18 rootless cittas There are 18 types of rootless consciousness:

a.) cittas which are unwholesome results:

1. body-consciousness accompanied by unpleasant feeling. 2. ear-consciousness 3. nose-consciousness accompanied by indifferent feeling. 4. tongue-consciousness 5. eye-consciousness 6. receiving-consciousness accompanied by indifferent feeling. 7. investigation-consciousness

b.) cittas which are wholesome results:

8. body-consciousness accompanied by pleasant feeling. 9. ear-consciousness 10. nose-consciousness accompanied by indifferent feeling. 11. tongue-consciousness 12. eye-consciousness 13. receiving-consciousness accompanied by indifferent feeling. 14. investigating-consciousness 15. investigating-consciousness accompanied by pleasant feeling.

c.) functional (kiriya) cittas:

accompanied by indifferent 16. five sense-door adverting consciousness feeling. 17. mind-door adverting consciousness accompanied by pleasant feeling. 18. smile-producing consciousness (of an arahant)

An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 33

The sensuous sphere: 24 beautiful cittas There are 24 types of beautiful (sobhana) cittas of the sensuous sphere:

a.) cittas which are wholesome consciousness (kusala):

1. citta, unprompted associated with 2. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by pleasant 3. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 4. citta, prompted wisdom 5. citta, unprompted associated with 6. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by indifferent 7. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 8. citta, prompted wisdom

b.) cittas which are wholesome result (kusala vipāka):

9. citta, unprompted associated with 10. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by pleasant 11. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 12. citta, prompted wisdom 13. citta, unprompted associated with 14. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by indifferent 15. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 16. citta, prompted wisdom

c.) cittas which are neutral (kiriya):

17. citta, unprompted associated with 18. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by pleasant 19. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 20. citta, prompted wisdom 21. citta, unprompted associated with 22. citta, prompted wisdom accompanied by indifferent 23. citta, unprompted feeling. dissociated with 24. citta, prompted wisdom

The form sphere: 15 cittas There are 15 types of form sphere consciousness (rūpāvacara citta) of the meditative absorptions:

a.) cittas which are wholesome consciousness:

first jhāna citta with initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness and one- 1. pointedness. second jhāna citta with sustained application, joy, happiness and one-pointedness. 2. third jhāna citta with joy, happiness and one-pointedness. 3. fourth jhāna citta with happiness and one-pointedness. 4. fifth jhāna citta with equanimity and one-pointedness. 5.

b.) cittas which are resultant consciousness:

first jhāna resultant citta with initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, 6. and one-pointedness. second jhāna resultant citta with sustained application, joy, happiness, and one- 7. pointedness. third jhāna resultant citta with joy, happiness and one-pointedness. 8. fourth jhāna resultant citta with happiness and one-pointedness. 9. fifth jhāna resultant citta with equanimity and one-pointedness. 10.

An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 35

c.) cittas which are neutral (kiriya) consciousness:

first jhāna kiriya citta with initial application, sustained application, joy, happiness, and 11. one-pointedness. second jhāna kiriya citta with sustained application, joy, happiness and one-pointedness. 12. third jhāna kiriya citta with joy, happiness and one-pointedness. 13. fourth jhāna kiriya citta with happiness and one-pointedness. 14. fifth jhāna kiriya citta with equanimity and one-pointedness. 15.

The formless sphere: 12 cittas There are 12 types of formless sphere consciousness (arūpāvacara citta) of the higher meditative absorptions:

a.) cittas which are wholesome consciousness:

jhāna citta dwelling on the ‘Infinity of Space’. 1. jhāna citta dwelling on the ‘Infinity of Consciousness’. 2. jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Nothingness’. 3. jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Neither Perception nor Non-perception’. 4.

b.) cittas which are resultant consciousness:

resultant jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Infinity of Space’. 5. resultant jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Infinity of Consciousness’. 6. resultant jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Nothingness’. 7. resultant jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Neither Perception nor Non-perception’. 8.

c.) cittas which are functional (kiriya) consciousness:

kiriya jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Infinity of Space’. 9. kiriya jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Infinity of Consciousness’. 10. kiriya jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Nothingness’. 11. kiriya jhāna citta dwelling on ‘Neither Perception nor Non-perception’. 12.

Page 35
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 36

The supramundane: 8 cittas There are 8 types of supramundane consciousness (lokuttara citta). These are the cittas of one who is experiencing the unconditioned reality, nibbāna:

a) cittas which are supramundane path consciousness (maggacitta):

sotāpanna path consciousness. 1. sakadāgāmi path consciousness. 2. anāgāmi path consciousness. 3. arahatta path consciousness. 4.

b) cittas which are resultant supramundane consciousness (phalacitta):

sotāpanna fruit consciousness. 5. sakadāgāmi fruit consciousness. 6. anāgāmi fruit consciousness. 7. arahatta fruit consciousness. 8.

Thus there are 89 different types of citta which can be experienced – 12 unwholesome cittas, 21 wholesome cittas, 36 resultant cittas and 20 functional cittas. In the sensuous sphere there are 54 types of citta, in the form sphere 15 types, in the formless sphere 12 types and in the supramundane sphere 8 types.

These different classes of cittas can also be divided into 121 types according to if the cittas of the path and fruit of Sotāpanna consciousness, Sakadāgāmi consciousness, Anāgāmi consciousness and Arahatta consciousness are accompanied by the jhāna factors of the first, second, third, fourth and fifth jhāna. Thus there are 16 additional types of maggacitta and 16 additional types of phalacitta.

Cetasikas: the 52 mental factors

The mental factors (cetasikas) which accompany moments of citta are of 52 different kinds. Of these 52, they are subdivided according to their natures into seven classes.

First there are the 7 universals (sabbacittasādhāraṇā). They accompany every single moment of citta and thus are called universals:

Page 36
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 37

contact (phassa) 1. 2. feeling (vedanā) perception (saññā) 3. volition or intention (cetanā) 4. one-pointedness (ekaggatā) 5. 6. psychic-life (jīvitindriya) attention (manasikāra) 7.

Then there are the 6 particular cetasikas, so called because they associate with only particular types of consciousness. They associate with either the wholesome or unwholesome cittas. They are called pakiṇṇaka in Pāḷi.

initial application (vitakka) 1. sustained application (vicāra) 2. determination (adhimokkha) 3. effort (viriya) 4. interest (pīti) 5. desire-to-do (chanda) 6.

Next are the 14 unwholesome cetasikas (akusala cetasikas). They make up all the akusala moments of consciousness.

Page 37
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 38

1. ignorance (moha) 2. lack of moral shame (ahirika) lack of fear of unwholesomeness (anottappa) 3. restlessness (uddhacca) 4. attachment (lobha) 5.

6. wrong view (diṭṭhi) conceit (māna) 7.

aversion (dosa) 8. 9. envy (issā) stinginess (macchariya) 10. regret (kukkucca) 11. sloth (thīna) 12. torpor (middha) 13. doubt (vicikicchā) 14.

Next are the 19 beautiful cetasikas (sobhanasādhāraṇā) so called because they are common to all morally beautiful moments of consciousness.

Page 38
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 39

1. confidence (saddhā) mindfulness (sati) 2. moral shame (hiri) 3. fear of unwholesomeness (ottappa) 4. disinterestedness (alobha) 5. amity (adosa) 6. equanimity (tatramajjhattatā) 7. composure of mental states (kāyapassaddhi) 8. composure of mind (cittapassaddhi) 9. lightness of mental states (kāya-lahutā) 10. lightness of mind (citta-lahutā) 11. pliancy of mental states (kāya-mudutā) 12. 13. pliancy of mind (citta-mudutā) adaptability of mental states (kāya-kammaññatā) 14. adaptability of mind (citta-kammaññatā) 15. proficiency of mental states (kāya-pāguññatā) 16. 17. proficiency of mind (citta-pāguññatā) rectitude of mental states (kāya-ujukatā) 18. rectitude of mind (citta-ujukatā). 19.

There are the 3 abstinences (virati cetasikas):

right speech (sammā vācā) 20. right action (sammā kammanta) 21. right livelihood (sammā ājīva) 22.

The two cetasikas called the illimitables (appamaññā), so called because their objects are without limit:

23. compassion (karuṇā) sympathetic joy (muditā). 24.

And finally the last sobhana cetasika:

25. wisdom (paññā).

Page 39
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 40

Thus there are 25 morally beautiful cetasikas (sobhana cetasikas) arising in various combinations in the wholesome states of consciousness. And a total of 52 different cetasikas that can arise in groups with the citta.

Rūpa: the 28 kinds of matter

We now come to the classification of matter. Rūpa or material phenomena consists of 8 basic constituents which compose all matter. These are known as the ‘eightfold group’ (suddhaṭṭhakakalāpa). These consist of the four great elements (mahābhūta) and four more derived from them (upādāya-rūpa).

solidity (paṭhavī) 1. 2. cohesion (āpo) temperature (tejo) 3. motion (vāyo) 4.

and the derivatives:

colour (vaṇṇa) 5. 6. smell (gandha) taste (rasa) 7. nutriment (ojā). 8.

There are a further 20 types of matter, all of which are also derived rūpas:

Page 40
An Introduction To The Abhidhamma The sensuous sphere: 12 unwholesome cittas (p. 31–42) p. 41

9. eye organ (cakkhu) 10. ear organ (sota) nose organ (ghāna) 11. tongue organ (jivhā) 12. 13. body organ (kāya) male and female characteristic – 2 rūpas (bhāva-rūpas) 14. heart base (hadayavatthu) 15. material life-principle (rūpa-jīvita) 16. 17. space (pariccheda) bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) 18. speech intimation (vacī-viññatti) 19. sound (sadda) 20. lightness (lahutā) 21. plasticity (mudutā) 22. adaptability (kammaññatā) 23. growth (upacaya) 24. continuity (santati) 25.

26. decay (jaratā) impermanence (aniccatā). 27.

These are all the different types of rūpa. The fourteenth type, male and female characteristic, is of two types which makes a total of 28 rūpas.

Thus concludes the appendix containing the classification of the varieties of nāma and rūpa (mental phenomena and material phenomena). There are 89 (or 121) types of consciousness, 52 different mental factors and 28 types of matter. The Buddha explained that these are the sum total of conditioned realities. There is one type of unconditioned reality and that is called nibbāna (in Sanskrit, nirvāṇa). Nibbāna is described as the ‘deathless’, the ‘cool’, the ‘incomparable’, the ‘peaceful’. It is the end of craving, the goal of the Buddha’s teachings.
